name: Nicotinamide riboside

lead: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a form of vitamin B3 that raises NAD+. People take it to support energy and slower aging, which they connect to healthier, younger-looking skin.

NR is converted to NMN and then to NAD+, supporting sirtuin and DNA-repair activity. Randomized trials consistently show it raises blood NAD+ metabolites, and trials in several conditions have mostly established tolerability. A 2023 review found it unclear whether raising NAD+ improves function in people, and appearance effects have not been tested.

paras: Taken as a daily capsule, often in longevity stacks alongside resveratrol, quercetin or NMN. Users usually report energy effects over several weeks.

Well tolerated in studies, with mild nausea, flushing or digestive effects at higher intakes. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US and novel food approval in the EU; product quality varies.

angle.text: Nicotinamide riboside is taken to raise NAD+, which users link to cellular energy, slower aging and a younger look. Human studies show it raises NAD+; visible aging effects have not been tested.

lead: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a pyridine-nucleoside and a form of vitamin B3 that serves as a precursor to the coenzyme NAD+ [1]. Inside cells it is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is then converted to NAD+ by NMNAT enzymes, bypassing other known NAD+ synthesis routes [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement under brands such as Tru Niagen and is closely related to, and often compared with, NMN [1][2].

People who take NR do so mainly for energy and healthy ageing, on the premise that NAD+ declines with age and that supplementing a precursor restores it [3][4]. The appearance-related ideas attached to it are indirect: more energy and cellular repair capacity are said to support training, recovery and a younger-looking skin and physique, although these links come from marketing and community discussion more than from trials of appearance outcomes. Randomised trials consistently show that oral NR raises blood NAD+ metabolites, and a 2023 review concluded that evidence that raising NAD+ improves physiological function in people is unclear [5]. Trials in conditions such as mild cognitive impairment, Parkinson's disease, COPD, kidney disease and peripheral artery disease have mostly established safety and tolerability, with variable functional effects [6][7][8][9][10].

The compound has a documented scientific history. Charles Brenner and Peter Bieganowski reported in a 2004 Cell paper that NR is a nutrient and that NRK genes provide a route to NAD+ in yeast and humans [11]. Commercial development followed from 2012 under ChromaDex (now Niagen Bioscience), and competing supplements such as Elysium Health's Basis launched in 2015 [1][12][13]. Brenner, who has served as chief scientific advisor to Niagen Bioscience, has said publicly that NR is not a longevity drug [14][15].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities NR appears in supplement lists, with some users reporting increased energy and others using it as part of longevity stacks alongside resveratrol and quercetin [16][17].

paras: The molecular weight of NR is 255.25 g/mol, and 290.70 g/mol for its chloride salt, so 100 mg of NR chloride supplies about 88 mg of NR [1]. NR chloride degrades above about 130 degrees Celsius into nicotinamide and ribose and breaks down faster at neutral than at acidic pH, which affects how it is formulated and stored [1].

NR was described in bacteria in 1944 as a growth factor for Haemophilus influenzae, which depends on salvage of NAD precursors from its environment [1]. Pellagra, the first disease linked to NAD deficiency, was tied to nutrition by Joseph Goldberger in 1914 and to niacin deficiency by Conrad Elvehjem in 1937, leading to identification of nicotinic acid and nicotinamide as precursors [1]. In 2004 NR was reported as an additional NAD precursor in eukaryotes, and it is now recognised as a vitamin B3 form present in cow and human milk [1].

ChromaDex licensed patents for NR from Dartmouth College, Cornell University and Washington University in St Louis in 2012 and developed a production process for NR chloride, branded Niagen. The company was in a patent dispute with Elysium Health over NR supplements between 2016 and 2023 and was renamed Niagen Bioscience in 2025 [1]. A 2016 Nature Communications paper reported that NR is orally bioavailable in mice and humans [18].

Brenner, a biochemist whose career has included Dartmouth, the University of Iowa and City of Hope, led the 2004 work; his page notes that he is chief scientific advisor of Niagen Bioscience and is a public sceptic of longevity claims, having described David Sinclair's book Lifespan as a source of longevity misinformation [14]. A 2016 Nature Communications paper reported that NR is orally bioavailable in mice and humans, and the first human trial of NR is listed as 2016 [18][14].

ChromaDex was founded in 1999 by Frank Jaksch as a reference-standards company. It acquired HealthSpan Research and its Tru Niagen consumer product in March 2017, and in 2018 Robert Fried became chief executive. It reports having supported more than 35 human clinical studies of its NR chloride, and it was renamed Niagen Bioscience in March 2025 [19].

Elysium Health was founded in 2014 by Leonard Guarente, Dan Alminana and Eric Marcotulli and launched Basis, a supplement combining NR and pterostilbene, in 2015. The company raised US$20 million in a December 2016 Series B round and has since added products for brain health, skin and collagen, and eye health [13].

The two companies became litigants. Wikipedia reports that ChromaDex sold the NR ingredient used in Basis and later sued Elysium; Dartmouth College and ChromaDex filed patent claims against Elysium in 2018, a district judge dismissed them in 2021, and in 2023 the Federal Circuit affirmed that the patents were invalid [13]. W. R. Grace also sued over crystalline NR patents in 2020 [13]. Wikipedia's ChromaDex article carries a notice that it contains promotional content and may need neutral revision [19].

Animal work forms the basis of much of the interest. A 2012 Cell Metabolism study reported that NR enhanced oxidative metabolism and protected mice against high-fat-diet-induced obesity, and a 2016 Science paper reported that NAD+ repletion with NR improved mitochondrial and muscle stem-cell function and extended lifespan in mice [20][21]. Reviews of NAD+ biology caution that animal results may not translate to humans [22][5].

In people, a 2018 Nature Communications trial of healthy middle-aged and older adults reported that chronic NR supplementation was well tolerated and elevated NAD+ [23]. A 2025 meta-analysis examined NMN and NR for skeletal muscle mass and function [24].

A 2022 paper in Biosensors and Bioelectronics by Maric and colleagues reported that in mice given an NR-rich diet and then injected with triple-negative breast cancer cells, 9 of 11 mice developed brain metastases versus 3 of 12 controls; tumour formation was not significantly different. The authors did not test whether NR raises the risk of cancer in cancer-free animals, and commentary notes the small sample [25]. A 2023 mouse study of hepatocellular carcinoma reported the opposite direction, with NR alleviating weight loss and lung metastasis. AARP quotes clinicians advising people who have or have had cancer to avoid NAD+ supplements while research continues [26].

NR is promoted for energy and healthy ageing rather than direct changes to appearance, and no published trial reviewed here measures facial or skin appearance outcomes. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis examined NMN and NR for skeletal muscle mass and function [24]. Forum users report taking NR for energy, with one describing the results as pricey but strong [17].

NR is not approved as a drug. It has been tested in clinical studies of neurological disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, peripheral artery disease, COPD, mitochondrial disease, ataxia-telangiectasia and lupus [6][7][8][9][10][27][28][29][30].

NAD+ is a coenzyme for redox reactions and a substrate for sirtuins, PARPs and CD38; its levels fall with age in several tissues in animal models, and restoring NAD+ in old or diseased animals has improved function and, in some models, lifespan [3][4]. NR and NMN are the two best-studied precursors, and reviews note they may behave differently depending on tissue expression of NAD-synthesising enzymes [2]. Reviews also caution that much of NAD+ biology is poorly understood and that animal results may not translate to humans [22][5].
A 2025 study reported that NR and NMN facilitate NAD+ synthesis through enterohepatic circulation, indicating that gut and liver processing shape how precursors reach tissues [31].

A 2023 review of human supplementation with NAD+-boosting compounds concluded that oral NR and NMN raise NAD+ levels but that the evidence that this improves physiological function is unclear [5]. A long-term randomised, placebo-controlled trial of NR chloride in healthy overweight adults assessed safety and metabolism [32].

In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a 10-week randomised pilot of 20 participants with dose escalation to 1 g per day had safety as its primary objective [6]. The NADPARK phase I trial gave 1,000 mg NR or placebo for 30 days to 30 newly diagnosed Parkinson's patients; NR was well tolerated and increased cerebral NAD levels, with variable response [7]. Randomised trials have also examined airway inflammation in COPD, a crossover of CoQ10 and NR in chronic kidney disease, and walking performance in peripheral artery disease [8][9][10]. A registered trial is testing NR for arterial stiffness and elevated blood pressure in advanced CKD [33]. Several registered studies in heart failure were small or terminated early [34][35][27].
No randomised trial among those reviewed tested NR for facial appearance or aesthetic outcomes.

Trials in healthy and diseased populations have generally reported that NR was well tolerated at the doses studied, with occasional mild nausea, flushing or digestive complaints reported with niacin-family compounds [6][7][32]. Long-term safety data beyond months are limited [5]. The US FDA accepted a GRAS notice for NR chloride in 2016 and recognised it as a new dietary ingredient in 2015 and 2017, and the EU authorised it as a novel food in food supplements in 2020; Wikipedia notes these decisions relied on safety sources supplied by the manufacturer [1].

The NR market has been shaped by patent litigation between ChromaDex and Elysium Health between 2016 and 2023 [1]. In forums, NR and NMN are often discussed interchangeably, with some users switching from NR to NMN because of cost [17]. One TRT forum user lists NR hydrogen malate alongside resveratrol, quercetin and beetroot in a daily regimen [16].

News coverage describes NAD+ products as a social-media trend. National Geographic reported in September 2025 that podcast hosts and health influencers promote NAD+ and that some clinics market NAD+ IV therapy as a longevity secret; in the same article Brenner said NR is 'not a longevity drug' and Columbia's David Seres said that 'thousands of anecdotes do not create evidence' [15].
AARP reported in November 2026 that influencers promote NAD+ supplements for longevity, and quoted Christopher Martens as saying sales are 'taking off well ahead of where the science is' [26].

lore.intro: NR is discussed in forums as a premium NAD+ booster for energy and longevity, frequently compared with NMN on price and effect [17]. Longevity influencers and IV clinics have extended the conversation beyond forums [15].
